strengths: The paper targets a real and underexplored evaluation setting: mathematical multiple-choice questions where answer options are separate images, requiring fine-grained visual comparison and text-image binding.
The benchmark size is meaningful for a focused evaluation: 1,800 questions and 8,070 images, with balanced answer positions and a useful split between stems with and without images.
The evaluation covers many contemporary LMMs, including closed, open, multi-image, and single-image models, and reports analyses by answer position and visual similarity quartile.
The examples suggest the task can expose failures that are not well captured by standard single-image math benchmarks.
weaknesses: There are serious internal inconsistencies in the experimental description and claims. The introduction says few-shot chain-of-thought prompting is used, while the experiment section says all models are evaluated zero-shot. The abstract/introduction also claims the best accuracy is GPT-4o at 45.9%, but the table reports higher results for Llama4-Maverick, Doubao, Gemini, and others. These issues undermine confidence in the reported evaluation.

The novelty claim is overstated. The paper acknowledges existing datasets with image-based answer options, including MV-Math and CMM-Math-test, but does not convincingly establish why VisioMath is categorically first rather than a larger or differently structured variant.

Dataset construction is insufficiently specified for a benchmark paper. The paper does not provide clear annotation protocols, inter-annotator agreement, quality-control statistics, error rates, category taxonomy, or examples of discarded/ambiguous cases.

Reproducibility is weak. The manuscript does not clearly state dataset release details, licensing for exam-derived images, evaluation code availability, exact prompts, model versions/API dates, image formatting, or response parsing validation. Using GLM4-Flash to extract answers introduces another model-dependent source of noise without adequate audit.

The evaluation lacks important baselines and controls, such as OCR-only/text-only variants, human performance, stronger prompt sensitivity analysis, repeated runs where nondeterminism exists, and validation that answer extraction does not bias results.

Several analyses are shallow or unsupported. Claims about positional bias, deep-thinking model degradation, and single-image architectural limitations are plausible but not rigorously tested; many are based on aggregate accuracy differences without statistical uncertainty or causal controls.

The benchmark may be vulnerable to data contamination because questions are sourced from public Chinese exams from 2002-2023, but the paper does not discuss contamination risk for closed or open models trained on web data.
Presentation quality is below top-tier standard, with typos, inconsistent dataset naming, unclear table formatting, contradictory numbers, and awkward writing that make the paper harder to trust.

strengths: The paper identifies a relevant evaluation niche: mathematical reasoning with image-based answer options, which is common in educational settings and not fully covered by many visual math benchmarks.
The dataset has a reasonable scale for a benchmark paper, with 1,800 questions and 8,070 images, balanced answer labels, and examples spanning several visual math formats.

The evaluation covers a broad set of LMMs, including closed-source, multi-image, and single-image models, and the paper attempts useful analyses by stem type, answer position, visual similarity, and merged-image variants.
weaknesses: The novelty is overstated. Prior datasets such as CMM-Math-test, Gaokao-MM-Math, and MV-Math already include multi-image and/or image-option math questions, so the contribution appears more incremental than the paper claims.

There are serious internal inconsistencies in the experimental description and claims. The introduction says the authors use chain-of-thought prompting with few-shot exemplars, while the experiment setup says all models are evaluated zero-shot with a unified prompt. The abstract highlights GPT-4o at 45.9% as if it were the strongest result, but Table 3 reports substantially higher results for Gemini2-flash, Doubao, and Llama4-Maverick.

The benchmark construction is under-specified. The paper does not provide enough detail on annotation guidelines, inter-annotator agreement, quality-control outcomes, train/test leakage checks, or whether the cropped exam questions can be legally redistributed.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently rigorous. There is no human baseline, no text-only/OCR-only baseline, no option-order randomization study, no statistical uncertainty, and no clear handling of model-specific image input constraints beyond simple concatenation for single-image models.

The response parsing pipeline uses GLM4-Flash to extract choices from model outputs, which introduces another model into the evaluation loop. The paper does not validate this extractor or report parsing error rates, making the reported accuracies less trustworthy.

Several analyses are weakly supported or possibly misinterpreted. The claimed positional bias appears to be inferred from accuracy conditioned on the ground-truth option rather than from prediction distributions, and the similarity analysis relies on Qwen embedding similarity without validation that it tracks human-perceived mathematical/visual difficulty.

The main empirical conclusions are often stronger than the evidence. For example, the paper attributes failures to multi-image reasoning limitations, but does not disentangle visual perception, Chinese language understanding, OCR, option binding, diagram parsing, and mathematical reasoning.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript does not include the exact prompts, decoding details for proprietary APIs, preprocessing scripts, image resolution policy, dataset release plan, or sufficient details to reproduce the benchmark and evaluations.

Presentation quality is poor for a top-tier submission. Several figures/tables render as unreadable glyphs in the PDF, there are typos and naming inconsistencies such as VisioMath/VisoMath and 'Anaysis', and some references/citations appear mismatched or noisy.

The paper does not address ethical and legal considerations around using exam materials from 2002-2023, including copyright, consent/permission, and potential benchmark contamination from publicly available exam PDFs.

strengths: Introduces a timely and practically relevant benchmark for multimodal mathematical reasoning where answer options are images, a setting that is common in exams but less directly covered by most prior math/VQA benchmarks.

The dataset is reasonably sized for this specialized setting, with 1,800 questions and 8,070 images, balanced answer positions, and a clear focus on fine-grained visual discrimination among similar options.
The empirical evaluation is broad, covering 36 proprietary and open-source LMMs across multi-image and single-image input settings, which gives a useful snapshot of current model limitations.

The paper provides informative analyses beyond aggregate accuracy, including performance by answer position, question stems with/without images, visual similarity quartiles, merged-image ablations, and option-labeling effects.
The results are compelling: even strong models remain far from saturated, suggesting the benchmark can be useful for diagnosing weaknesses in multi-image visual grounding and mathematical reasoning.
weaknesses: The novelty is positive but somewhat overstated: related benchmarks such as MV-Math and CMM-Math already include multi-image or image-option math settings, so the paper should position the exact distinction more carefully and empirically.

Reproducibility details are incomplete. The prompt template, image ordering/formatting, response parser validation, invalid-rate statistics, and dataset release/licensing details are not sufficiently specified for a benchmark paper.

There is an inconsistency in the evaluation description: the introduction mentions chain-of-thought prompting with few-shot exemplars, while the experiment setup states zero-shot evaluation with a unified prompt.

The benchmark is sourced from public Chinese exams from 2002-2023, raising possible contamination concerns for commercial and open models; the paper does not provide a memorization/leakage analysis or a held-out newly authored subset.

Dataset quality claims rely mostly on manual review statements, but the paper lacks inter-annotator agreement, expert validation statistics, category taxonomy, difficulty labels, or human performance estimates.

The use of GLM4-Flash to extract answers from model responses may introduce evaluator bias or parsing errors; the paper should report manual audit results or use a deterministic extraction protocol where possible.
Some analyses make broad causal claims, such as architectural deficiencies or deep-thinking degradation causes, from correlational accuracy patterns without enough supporting evidence.
The presentation has several polish issues, including typos, inconsistent naming, and occasional unclear table/figure descriptions, which slightly weakens confidence in the benchmark documentation.

strengths: Addresses a timely and underexplored evaluation setting: mathematical multiple-choice problems where the answer options themselves are visually similar diagrams, requiring fine-grained cross-image comparison and text-image grounding.
The benchmark is reasonably sized for a specialized curated dataset, with 1,800 problems and 8,070 option images drawn from real exam-style sources, and it covers several K-12 math subdomains.

The empirical evaluation is broad, including many closed-source and open-source LMMs, multiple model scales, single-image and multi-image settings, and analyses by answer position, stem-image presence, and visual similarity quartile.
The paper identifies practically relevant failure modes such as option-image misalignment and positional heuristics, and the shuffling and visual-anchor experiments are useful probes of this issue.
The proposed mitigation strategies are simple and informative; especially the explicit option anchors and small CoT fine-tuning study suggest plausible directions for improving multi-image alignment.
weaknesses: The benchmark construction details are insufficient for a dataset paper at this venue. The paper claims expert annotation and cross-validation but gives little information about annotator qualifications, annotation protocol, disagreement rates, inter-annotator agreement, quality-control statistics, or how translated English versions were produced and verified.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper describes prompts and some hyperparameters, but it does not clearly commit to releasing the dataset, image crops, code, evaluation scripts, model outputs, or answer-extraction validation. For a benchmark contribution, this is a major concern.

The copyright and licensing situation is under-addressed. The benchmark is derived from Chinese exam papers and an additional internet-crawled CoT dataset, but the ethics statement only says the data are publicly available and legally compliant; it does not clarify redistribution rights, licenses, or whether copyrighted exam diagrams can be released.

The central causal claim that higher visual similarity causes performance degradation is not fully supported. Similarity quartiles may be confounded by topic, problem difficulty, visual complexity, stem-image presence, OCR/translation quality, or diagram type. No controlled matching, regression, or stratified analysis is provided.

The visual similarity metric is weakly justified. Minimum pairwise cosine similarity from Qwen multimodal embeddings may capture semantic/category similarity rather than fine-grained visual confusability; the paper does not validate the metric against human judgments or alternative perceptual metrics.

The error analysis is too small and narrow: only 50 errors from one model are manually categorized, with no annotation protocol, no inter-rater reliability, and inconsistent wording about five versus four error types. This is not enough to support broad claims about dominant failure modes across LMMs.

The option-shuffling experiment is suggestive but not cleanly diagnostic. Changing the prompt to a nonstandard order may introduce prompt-following difficulty or confusion, not only reveal positional heuristics. More controls are needed, such as randomized image orders, embedded labels, and per-model prompt-sensitivity checks.

The improvement experiments are limited. Strategy 3 is evaluated only on Qwen2.5-VL-3B, uses synthetic rationales generated by stronger models, and lacks ablations separating captioning, CoT, answer filtering, option shuffling, and data volume. Possible train-test contamination from internet-crawled math problems is not ruled out.

Several reported results reveal strong answer-position biases and near-random performance for many open-source models, but the paper does not deeply analyze invalid outputs, extraction errors, confidence intervals, or statistical significance.

The presentation has notable polish issues, including table formatting problems, typos, inconsistent model names, and some overclaiming such as calling VisioMath the first benchmark for this setting without a more careful positioning against CMM-Math-test and MV-Math.

strengths: The paper targets a relevant and underexplored evaluation setting: math questions where answer choices are visually similar diagrams, which is a genuine challenge for multimodal models.
The benchmark is moderately sized, uses real exam-style problems, balances answer positions, and includes both Chinese and English prompts/examples.
The evaluation covers a broad set of closed-source and open-source LMMs and reports useful breakdowns by stem-image presence, answer position, and option-image similarity.
The paper includes some diagnostic experiments, such as option shuffling and visual-textual anchoring, that point toward plausible alignment failures in current models.
weaknesses: The novelty is incremental for a top-tier venue: the core contribution is mainly a curated benchmark variant of multimodal math/multi-image QA, and the paper does not convincingly establish that it is conceptually distinct from or substantially stronger than existing multi-image math benchmarks beyond having more figure-based options.

Dataset quality and reproducibility are insufficiently documented. The paper gives little detail on annotation protocol, annotator expertise, inter-annotator agreement, translation quality, filtering criteria, image-cropping quality control, licensing/copyright of exam materials, or whether the benchmark and code will actually be released.

The risk of data contamination is serious and under-addressed. The items come from public Chinese entrance exams from 2002-2023, which are likely present in web-scale pretraining corpora, yet the paper provides no leakage analysis. This undermines claims about reasoning ability, especially for closed-source frontier models.

The visual-similarity analysis is not technically convincing. Similarity is defined as the minimum pairwise cosine similarity under one embedding model, but there is no validation that this metric reflects human-perceived diagram similarity or task difficulty, and several conclusions rely heavily on this measurement.

The evaluation methodology has weaknesses: accuracy alone is reported; there are no confidence intervals or statistical tests; answer extraction relies on another LLM; invalid-output rates are not reported; prompt sensitivity is not examined; and the setup may advantage/disadvantage models depending on their multi-image API formatting.

The central claim that image-text misalignment is the dominant failure mode is weakly supported. The error analysis uses only 50 erroneous cases from one model, lacks inter-rater reliability, and is not repeated across stronger models. The paper also inconsistently says five error types while presenting four.

The mitigation experiments are preliminary and overclaimed. Strategies 1 and 2 are input-format tricks rather than algorithmic contributions, and Strategy 3 is tested only on a single small model with synthetic LLM-generated CoT data, no ablations for data source/size/labels, no held-out contamination check, and no comparison to standard SFT baselines.

Several reported findings are less strong than the prose suggests. Some models remain robust under high similarity, and the performance drops may partly reflect model capability, image resolution, prompt formatting, or dataset composition rather than a specific alignment mechanism.

The paper’s presentation has many quality issues: grammatical errors, malformed table extraction/formatting, inconsistent model names, typos such as “Lable” and “Vison,” and imprecise claims. This hurts confidence in the care of the benchmark construction and evaluation.

The ethics and broader-impact discussion is superficial. It asserts legal compliance for exam materials without evidence, and does not adequately discuss benchmark release rights, possible memorization of copyrighted educational content, or language/curriculum bias.

strengths: The paper targets a clear and underexplored evaluation setting: mathematical multiple-choice problems where all options are visually similar diagrams. This is a meaningful gap in current multimodal math benchmarks.

VisioMath appears practically valuable: 1,800 curated K-12 exam-style problems, balanced answer positions, bilingual presentation, and independent option images create a focused testbed for fine-grained multi-image reasoning.

The empirical evaluation is broad, covering many closed-source, open-source multi-image, and single-image LMMs, with useful breakdowns by stem-image presence, answer position, and visual similarity quartile.

The findings are coherent and actionable: performance drops with visual similarity, image-containing stems are harder, option shuffling exposes brittle image-text binding, and explicit anchors or layout consolidation improve performance.
The paper goes beyond benchmarking by providing error analysis and mitigation experiments, including a small alignment-oriented CoT fine-tuning study with a substantial gain on Qwen2.5-VL-3B.
weaknesses: The novelty is mainly benchmark construction plus empirical analysis rather than a new modeling method; the mitigation strategies are sensible but relatively simple and not deeply developed.

Dataset construction details are still insufficient for full reproducibility: the paper does not clearly specify public release status, licensing/copyright handling for exam materials, translation process, annotator agreement statistics, or how many items were removed at each filtering stage.

The visual similarity metric is based on a single embedding model and the minimum pairwise cosine similarity; this may not reliably capture human-perceived confusability or task-relevant diagram similarity, and no validation of the metric is provided.
The error analysis is based on only 50 errors from one model, which is too small to strongly support broad claims about dominant failure modes across LMMs.

The fine-tuning result is promising but limited: it is shown for only one small model, without held-out contamination checks against the benchmark, comparison to non-CoT or non-alignment SFT controls, or analysis of whether gains come from better reasoning versus domain adaptation.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence supports, such as attributing failures primarily to image-text misalignment when vision recognition, reasoning, and knowledge errors are also substantial and only manually assessed on a small sample.

Presentation has notable rough edges, including grammar issues, inconsistent terminology, table formatting/extraction artifacts, and some confusing dataset statistics such as whether 8,070 images refer to options only or all stem/options images.
